newsitem.title: USA: Clinton confers with Mubarak on Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton confers with Mubarak on Hebron deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton spoke by telephone with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday about the Israeli-Palestinian talks on the West Bank town of Hebron, the White House said on Monday.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry disclosed the contact as signs mounted that agreement on an Israeli withdrawal from Hebron was near. McCurry told reporters there had been progress in the talks, but said differences still remained.
Clinton called Mubarak "to exchange views with him on the status of the dialogue" and get Mubarak's insights "into the thinking of those who are negotiating," McCurry said.
Egypt has blamed Israel for the tortoise-like pace of the talks, saying Israel had taken rigid positions and had tried to put pressure on the Palestinian negotiators.

A PLO official said negotiators, meeting at a Jerusalem hotel, could conclude a deal within hours thanks to a compromise reached on Sunday for Israel to complete three troop withdrawals from still-occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.
The compromise was hammered out during a lightning mediation mission by Jordan's King Hussein.

McCurry said Clinton had received regular reports on the talks from U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross, deputy national security adviser Samuel Berger and others, and had "offered some thoughts" on how to resolve differences that have been stalling an agreement.

Cautioning reporters against being "excessively forward-leaning", McCurry said: "We are not encouraging people to leap to exuberant degrees of optimism. This is a process that requires hard work. Some progress has been made but there are differences that remain between the parties."

Israeli ambassador to the United States Eliahu Ben Elissar said he had spoken by telephone on Monday with one of the Israeli negotiators, "who told me that his impression was that the agreement was not going to be signed today".

"But it will be signed, if not today, it will be signed tomorrow, if not tomorrow, it will be signed the day after tomorrow," Ben Elissar told a meeting of the international Jewish organisation B'nai B'rith in Washington.

The Israeli envoy accused Palestinian President Yasser Arafat of "using as a political tool and as a full component of his strategy and his tactics, threats of violence and sometimes violence itself".
"This is what brings us to be more cautious, more prudent," he said.
